p.src:
The model $H=cP$ was useful because its wave packets translate without changing shape. It also carries a serious warning. Momentum may be positive or negative, so the same formula assigns positive energy to one plane wave and negative energy to the other: $\psi_p(x)=e^{ipx/\hbar},
\qquad
E(p)=cp.$ If arbitrarily many physical particles could occupy negative-energy states, empty space would not be the state of lowest energy. It could produce positive-energy quanta while depositing compensating negative energy into new particles, preserving total energy but lowering the vacuum without bound.

ja: ディラックの歴史的な答えはフェルミオンに対して有効であった。フェルミオンは排他原理に従う。すなわち、二つの同一なフェルミオンが同じ一粒子状態を占めることはできない。すべての負エネルギーの状態を埋め尽くすと想像しよう。それらがすべて占められると、排他原理によって別のフェルミオンがその領域へ落ち込むことが妨げられる。埋め尽くされた集合の中の空孔は反粒子として振る舞う。

p.src:
For one particle on a line, the position-space wave function is $\psi(x)=\braket{x}{\psi},$ the amplitude for finding the particle near $x$. The momentum-space wave function is $\widetilde{\psi}(p)=\braket{p}{\psi}.$ They describe the same abstract state in different bases and are related by a Fourier transform: $\begin{aligned}\psi(x)
&=
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
\frac{dp}{\sqrt{2\pi\hbar}}\,
\widetilde{\psi}(p)e^{ipx/\hbar},
\\
\widetilde{\psi}(p)
&=
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
\frac{dx}{\sqrt{2\pi\hbar}}\,
\psi(x)e^{-ipx/\hbar}.
\end{aligned}$

p.src: In two spatial dimensions, $X$ and $Y$ commute, so a common eigenbasis may be labeled by both coordinates and the wave function becomes $\psi(x,y)$. A macroscopic system can therefore require an enormous number of coordinates.

Light particles are more readily spread or diffracted by microscopic structure. This is a scaling argument, not a claim that mass alone decides whether motion is classical.
